user: Why would losing the line Bus_28 -> Bus_29 be critical at 18:00 on 6 January when it was not at 15:00?

grid.name: PGLib IEEE 30-Bus System (Alsac–Stott)
grid.description: Synthetic 7-day profile generated from the bundled PGLib IEEE 30-bus (Alsac–Stott) MATPOWER case: five dispatchable units with their own costs, line ratings from PGLib.

rating_mva.from: its current rating at the line's voltage

result.narrowed: Asked about the whole grid; Bus_29 is the only element outside its limits, so its own voltage was investigated.

classical.note: Classical views, beside the exact shares: they inform, the verdicts are the exact ones.

drill_down.note: Measured with the other factors as they are now.

result.message: Bus_29 is at 0.931 p.u. at 2000-01-06 18:00 after losing Bus_28 -> Bus_29 [L38], outside its limit (0.950 p.u.); at 2000-01-06 15:00 after losing Bus_28 -> Bus_29 [L38] (the moment asked for) it was 0.952 p.u. Of the 0.021 p.u. fall: Demand near Bus_29 (2 buses) 78 %; Demand elsewhere (19 buses) 22 %. The main cause is demand against every reference checked (the reference asked for 78 %; the last moment within limits 78 %; a moment well inside the limits 79 %; the day before 78 %).

data_check.message: The measured changes behind the causes look physical: no unusual jump, level or frozen value.

reference_robustness.message: The main cause is demand against every reference checked (the reference asked for 78 %; the last moment within limits 78 %; a moment well inside the limits 79 %; the day before 78 %).

recommended_action.text: No movement is certain to clear Bus_29. The smallest single-source option is a 591.02 MW increase of Gen_bus7, which works only if Gen_bus7 has that headroom — not known here. Check its capability, or use several sources.

the set-point 1.155 p.u. is outside the voltage band; Gen_bus12 would need 60.7 Mvar, outside -15 to 60 Mvar; it puts Bus_11, Bus_12, Bus_13, Bus_14, Bus_15, Bus_22, Bus_23 outside its limits

result.method: Every combination of the factors, each at its value now or in the reference state, was solved by AC power flow. A factor's share is its Shapley value — its average effect over every order in which the changes could have happened — so the shares add up to the change, interactions included.

load_power_factor.applies_to: measured loads (Q = P·tan(acos pf)); the nominal point keeps the case's own Q

assistant:
The outage is the same in both cases: **Bus_28 → Bus_29 [L38]**. The difference is the operating condition. At **15:00**, Bus_29 is at **0.952 p.u.** after the outage—only **0.002 p.u. above** the 0.950 limit. At **18:00**, it falls to **0.931 p.u.**, **0.019 p.u. below** the limit.

The main change is rising demand:

- Demand at Bus_28 and Bus_29 increased from **10.50 MW to 12.77 MW**. This local increase accounts for **78.4%** of the voltage drop.
- Demand elsewhere increased from **218.41 MW to 265.66 MW**, accounting for another **21.6%**.
- Changes in the five units’ output were ruled out as a meaningful cause.

So the line outage leaves Bus_29 with little voltage margin even at 15:00; by 18:00, higher local and system-wide demand pushes it below the limit. This conclusion held across the reference states checked. Reactive demand was derived using the default **0.95 lagging power factor**.

📋 Data source: measurements
